prompt: `actionMatches(pattern, action)` checks an IAM `Action` pattern against an API action. `*` matches any characters (so `s3:*` and `s3:Get*` work), and action names are case-insensitive. Fix it.
`arn_parts(arn)` splits an ARN (`arn:partition:service:region:account:resource`) into a dict. The resource part may itself contain `:` (Lambda: `function:my-fn`). Fix it.
Notes for setting up AWS access for a new team of four developers.

task.prompt: Mark the steps that go against IAM best practice.

segments.text: Turn on MFA for every human sign-in.
Store the root account email and password in the team password manager so anyone can use it in an emergency.
segments.issue: Root should be locked away with MFA and used almost never, not shared with the team.

segments.text: Put developers in a group and attach policies to the group, not to each person.
Give everyone `AdministratorAccess` so nobody gets blocked.
segments.issue: Violates least privilege; grant what each job needs and add more on request.

segments.text: Give EC2 instances a role instead of putting access keys on disk.
Review unused permissions each quarter using last-accessed data.

prompt: A new Lambda function must read items from one DynamoDB table, `orders`.

items.label: Create an execution role whose trust policy lets `lambda.amazonaws.com` assume it
Attach a policy allowing `dynamodb:GetItem` and `dynamodb:Query` on the `orders` table ARN
Set the function to use that role
Invoke the function and check CloudWatch Logs for `AccessDenied`

task.explanation: The role must exist and have permissions before the function can use it; then test.

prompt: The CLI says you are not allowed.

task.prompt: You run `aws s3 ls s3://acme-reports` and get `AccessDenied`, though your colleague says your user has read access.

steps.question: What do you run first?
options: `aws sts get-caller-identity` to see which identity the CLI is using
`aws iam create-access-key` to get fresh keys
Reinstall the AWS CLI
Ask for `AdministratorAccess`
steps.explanation: Most "I have access" mismatches come from the CLI using a different profile or role than you think.

steps.question: It shows an old `sandbox` profile. What fixes it?
options: Use the right profile: `--profile work` or set `AWS_PROFILE=work`
Delete the bucket policy
Add the sandbox user to the admin group
Wait for IAM to propagate for an hour
steps.explanation: Pick the intended credentials explicitly; no permission change is needed.

prompt: This policy is meant to let a reporting job **read** files in the `reports` bucket.

task.prompt: Mark the lines that grant more than that.

segments.issue: Reading needs only `s3:GetObject`; `s3:DeleteObject` lets the job delete reports.

prompt: What is the main difference between an IAM role and an IAM user?

options: A role has no long-term password or keys; whoever assumes it gets temporary credentials
A role can only be used by the root user
A user cannot have policies attached
Roles only work inside the AWS console
mcq.explanation: Roles are assumed by people, services or other accounts, and hand out short-lived credentials.

prompt: A user's only policy allows `s3:GetObject`. They call `ec2:RunInstances`. What happens?

options: Denied: anything not explicitly allowed is implicitly denied
Allowed, because no policy denies it
Allowed for 1 hour
The call is queued for an admin to approve
mcq.explanation: IAM denies by default. Without an Allow for the action, the request fails.

prompt: A GitHub Actions workflow needs to deploy to AWS. What is the best way to give it credentials?

options: Let it assume a role through GitHub's OIDC provider, getting short-lived credentials
Store an IAM user's access key as a repository secret
Commit the access key to a private repo
Use the root account's keys
mcq.explanation: OIDC federation removes long-lived keys entirely; each run gets temporary credentials for a scoped role.

prompt: `evaluate(statements, action)` returns `"Allow"`, `"ExplicitDeny"` or `"ImplicitDeny"` for one action. Each statement has `Effect` and `Action` (a string or a list, wildcards allowed via `matches`). An explicit Deny always wins, no matter the order. Fix it.

`find_wildcards(policy)` lists the `Sid`s (sorted) of **Allow** statements that are too broad: an action of `*` or a whole service (`s3:*`), or a resource of `*`. `Action` and `Resource` may be a string or a list. Fix it.
The trust policy of the role your GitHub Actions deploy job assumes via OIDC.

task.prompt: Mark the line that lets the wrong callers in.

segments.issue: Any repository on GitHub can assume this role. Pin it, e.g. `repo:acme/api:ref:refs/heads/main`.

prompt: An app uses an IAM user's access key and you must rotate it without downtime.

items.label: Create a second access key for the user
Deploy the app with the new key
Check the old key's last-used time to confirm nothing still uses it
Delete the old key after a waiting period

task.explanation: A user can hold two keys, so the new one goes live before the old one stops. Deactivating before deleting gives you an undo.

prompt: A developer should manage only their team's servers.

task.prompt: Developers on the web team must be able to start and stop EC2 instances tagged `team=web`, and no others.

steps.question: How do you express this in IAM?
options: Allow `ec2:StartInstances` and `ec2:StopInstances` with a condition `aws:ResourceTag/team` equals `web`
List every instance ID in the policy and update it on each launch
Give them `ec2:*` and ask them to be careful
Use a separate AWS account for every instance
steps.explanation: Tag-based conditions (ABAC) follow the tags, so new instances need no policy change.

steps.question: Testing shows they can still terminate any instance. Why?
options: Another policy attached to them (for example through a group) allows it; permissions from all attached policies add up
Conditions are ignored for EC2
Terminate is always allowed for the instance owner
IAM changes take a day to apply
steps.explanation: Effective permissions are the union of all Allows (minus Denies). Find the broad policy and remove it or add a Deny.

prompt: A Node.js service that reads files from S3, as written in a PR.

task.prompt: Mark the lines that leak or hard-code credentials.

segments.issue: Hard-coded keys end up in git; let the SDK pick up the instance or task role.
Logs every environment variable, including any secrets.

segments.text: const res = await s3.send(new GetObjectCommand({ Bucket, Key }));

prompt: A user is in a group whose policy allows `s3:*`. Their own user policy denies `s3:DeleteObject`. Can they delete objects?

options: No: an explicit Deny overrides any Allow
Yes: group policies win over user policies
Yes: the more recent policy wins
Only in buckets they created
mcq.explanation: Policy order and attachment point do not matter; any matching explicit Deny wins.

prompt: A role's identity policy allows `iam:*` and `s3:*`. Its permissions boundary allows only `s3:*`. What can the role do?

options: Only S3 actions: effective permissions are the intersection of the policy and the boundary
IAM and S3 actions
Nothing: a boundary blocks everything it does not deny
Only IAM actions
mcq.explanation: A boundary sets the maximum; it grants nothing on its own and caps what identity policies allow.

prompt: Launching an EC2 instance with an instance profile fails with an error about `iam:PassRole`. What does that permission control?

options: Whether you may hand a role to an AWS service, such as attaching it to an instance
Whether you may change your own password
Whether a role may assume another role
Whether you may read IAM policies
mcq.explanation: `iam:PassRole` stops people from giving a service a more powerful role than they have themselves.

prompt: `evaluate(statements, action, resource)` now checks resources too: a statement applies only if one of its `Action` patterns matches the action **and** one of its `Resource` patterns matches the resource. Use `matches` for both (wildcards). Explicit Deny wins. Fix the resource check.

`conditions_match(condition, context)` evaluates an IAM `Condition` block against request context keys. Supported operators: `StringEquals`, `StringLike` (with `*`), `Bool`. **Every** operator and key must match (AND); a list of values for one key means any of them (OR). A key missing from the context does not match. An empty condition matches. Fix it.
The permissions policy for the CI role that deploys the static site. Each line is one statement.

task.prompt: Mark the statements that let the CI role escalate its own privileges.

segments.issue: Can hand any role, including admin roles, to a service it controls. Scope it to the one role it must pass.
Can mint keys for any user, including admins.

prompt: AWS evaluates a request from a role in an account that belongs to an AWS Organization.

task.prompt: Put the checks in the order AWS's policy evaluation logic applies them.

items.label: Any explicit Deny in any applicable policy
Service control policies (SCPs) of the organization

task.explanation: Explicit denies are checked first and end the evaluation. Then SCPs, resource-based policies, identity-based policies and permissions boundaries, as in AWS's evaluation flowchart.

prompt: CI in a tools account deploys into the prod account.

task.prompt: A CI role in the tools account (111111111111) must deploy to prod (222222222222) by assuming the role `deployer` there.

steps.question: What must be in place?
options: `deployer`'s trust policy names the CI role's ARN, and the CI role has `sts:AssumeRole` on `deployer`'s ARN
Only the CI role's `sts:AssumeRole` permission
Only `deployer`'s trust policy
An access key for `deployer` stored in the tools account
steps.explanation: Assuming a cross-account role needs both: the target trusts the caller, and the caller is allowed to assume it.

steps.question: AssumeRole now works, but `s3:PutObject` to the prod bucket returns `AccessDenied`. Where do you look?
options: The `deployer` role's permissions, the bucket policy, and any SCP on the prod account
The CI role's S3 permissions in the tools account
The GitHub repository settings
The tools account's root user
steps.explanation: After AssumeRole the request is made as `deployer`, so prod-side policies decide.

prompt: A PR description for a new support role.

task.prompt: Mark the changes that are not least privilege.

segments.text: New role `support-readonly` with the AWS managed `ViewOnlyAccess` policy.
Adds `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` on `*` so support can debug config issues.
segments.issue: Lets support read every secret in the account, including database passwords.

segments.text: Started from a copy of the admin role's inline policy and removed the lines that looked dangerous.
segments.issue: A deny-by-memory approach; start from nothing and add only what support needs.

prompt: An SCP on a member account denies `ec2:*` when `aws:RequestedRegion` is not in the EU. A user there with `AdministratorAccess` calls `ec2:RunInstances` in `us-east-1`. What happens?

options: Denied: SCPs limit every principal in the account, admins included
Allowed: AdministratorAccess overrides SCPs
Allowed, but logged as a warning
Denied only if the user lacks MFA
mcq.explanation: SCPs set the maximum permissions for the account; an explicit Deny there applies to everyone except the management account.

prompt: In the **same** account, a bucket policy allows IAM user `alice` to `s3:GetObject`. Alice's own policies do not mention S3. Can she read objects?

options: Yes: within one account, an Allow in either the resource-based or the identity-based policy is enough
No: she also needs an identity policy
Only through a presigned URL
Only if the bucket is public
mcq.explanation: For same-account access to an IAM user, policies are combined; an Allow in the bucket policy suffices when nothing denies.

prompt:
What does this statement do?

```json
{ "Effect": "Allow", "NotAction": "iam:*", "Resource": "*" }
```

options: Allows every action except IAM actions; IAM actions are simply not allowed by this statement
Denies all IAM actions, even if another policy allows them
Allows only IAM actions
It is invalid; NotAction only works with Deny
mcq.explanation: `NotAction` with Allow grants everything not listed. It does not deny the listed actions; another policy could still allow them.

prompt: `escalationRisks(actions)` takes the action patterns a policy allows (wildcards allowed, case-insensitive) and returns which entries of `RISKY` they grant, in `RISKY` order. Fix it: `iam:*`, `iam:Put*` or `*` must count too.

`effective(identity, boundary, scp, action)` says whether a role may perform `action`. Each argument is a list of statements `{Effect, Action}` (`Action` is a string or list; use `_decide`). `boundary` is `None` when the role has no permissions boundary. The action is allowed only if no layer denies it and **every** layer present allows it. Fix it.
A role a third-party analytics vendor (account 999988887777) assumes to read your exports.

task.prompt: Mark the parts that put you at risk.

segments.issue: No `sts:ExternalId` check, so the vendor can be tricked into using this role for another customer (confused deputy).
Bucket-level `s3:*` includes `PutBucketPolicy` and `DeleteBucket`; listing needs only `s3:ListBucket`.

prompt: Your company still has 40 IAM users with long-lived access keys. You are moving everyone to IAM Identity Center (SSO).

task.prompt: Put the migration steps in order.

items.label: Inventory every user, access key and its last-used date
Set up Identity Center with permission sets per job function
Move people over to SSO and confirm they can work
Deactivate the old users' keys and watch for breakage
Delete the old users and add an SCP denying `iam:CreateUser` and `iam:CreateAccessKey`

task.explanation: Know what exists, build the replacement, move people, switch off the old path reversibly, then remove it and stop it coming back.

prompt: CloudTrail shows something odd.

task.prompt: A developer role, `dev-sandbox`, is allowed `iam:CreatePolicyVersion` on `*`. CloudTrail shows it called `CreatePolicyVersion` with `SetAsDefault: true` on a policy attached to itself, then created IAM users.

steps.question: What happened?
options: Privilege escalation: it rewrote its own attached policy to grant itself more access
A normal IAM policy update by AWS
A bug in CloudTrail
The role assumed the root user
steps.explanation: Being able to publish a new default version of your own policy is equivalent to granting yourself anything.

steps.question: What do you do first?
options: Revoke the role's active sessions and remove its IAM write permissions
Delete the CloudTrail logs to reduce noise
Wait to see what it does next
Rotate the root password only
steps.explanation: Revoking sessions invalidates credentials already issued; then remove the permission that allowed it.

steps.question: How do you prevent it for roles that developers create in future?
options: Require a permissions boundary on those roles that excludes IAM write actions
Ask developers not to use IAM
Turn off CloudTrail
Give every role `ReadOnlyAccess` on top
steps.explanation: A boundary caps what a role can ever do, even if its own policy is rewritten.

prompt: One bucket holds files for many customers (tenants).

task.prompt: Each tenant's files live under `s3://acme-tenants/{tenantId}/`. Your app assumes a role per request and passes the tenant ID as a session tag `tenant`.

steps.question: How do you limit each session to its tenant's prefix with one policy?
options: Resource `arn:aws:s3:::acme-tenants/${aws:PrincipalTag/tenant}/*`
One IAM role per tenant, created by hand
Check the prefix in the frontend
A bucket policy listing every tenant ID
steps.explanation: Policy variables with session tags (ABAC) give one policy that scales to any number of tenants.

steps.question: What must you also control?
options: Who may set the `tenant` session tag, so callers cannot tag themselves as another tenant
The S3 storage class of each tenant
The number of objects per prefix
Nothing else; tags are always trustworthy
steps.explanation: If any caller can choose its own tag value, the isolation is gone. Restrict `sts:TagSession` to your trusted app.

prompt: A bucket policy contains `"Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalOrgID": "o-abc123" } }` on an Allow. What does it do?

options: Limits the Allow to principals from accounts in your AWS Organization
Grants access to every account in the world
Encrypts objects with the organization's key
Requires MFA for organization members
mcq.explanation: `aws:PrincipalOrgID` lets you grant to the whole org without listing every account ID.

prompt: Why does a third-party vendor ask you to put an `sts:ExternalId` condition in the role you create for them?

options: To stop another of their customers from tricking the vendor into accessing your account (the confused deputy problem)
To encrypt the session
To make the role work across regions
To avoid CloudTrail logging
mcq.explanation: The external ID ties the role to your contract with the vendor, so knowing your role ARN is not enough.

prompt: A policy allows `s3:*` on `arn:aws:s3:::home/${aws:username}/*`. What can IAM user `alice` reach?

options: Only objects under `home/alice/`
Every object under `home/`
Nothing; variables are not allowed in resources
Objects of any user whose name she knows
mcq.explanation: `${aws:username}` is replaced with the caller's user name at evaluation time.
